# Corrected mode: what the switch "errors of the original" changes

Since v0.1.34 the apps listed here have a switch beside "Initial settings": **errors of the original: kept | corrected**.

- **kept** (the default) is the faithful port: every number and picture is what the original Demonstration gives,
  including the errors found in it (each app's `DESIGN.md` §11).
- **corrected** changes only the code needed to correct the findings listed below. Everything else — controls,
  layout, texts, the other findings — is the same in both modes.
- "Initial settings" returns to **kept**. A saved state or link without the variable `errata` is the original.
- The corrections are the port's; none has been confirmed by an author of the originals. The same list is on each
  page under "Errors of the original: what "corrected" changes".

To go back to the last version without the switch: tag `pre-fixed-mode-v0.1.33` (= v0.1.33, commit `b4569b0`).

Apps with the switch: 26; corrections: 47. Code version 0.1.40.

## Motion Planning for Robot Path around Obstacles (`demos/motion-planning/`)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| E-MP-01 | the search named A* adds the distance of a vertex to itself (always 0) as its estimate, so it is Dijkstra's algorithm. | the estimate is the straight distance from the vertex to the goal (A*). The path has the same length; between equally short routes another one may be drawn. |
| E-MP-02 | in the rotational sweep, two vertices on one ray from the sweep point are ordered by comparing a distance with an angle. | on the same ray the nearer vertex comes first. Visibility lines can change only in scenes with such collinear vertices. |
| E-MP-03 | the test "is the segment from a collinear previous vertex blocked?" is written with the wrong argument shape and never runs: the vertex behind it simply inherits the previous answer. | the test runs: a vertex behind a collinear one is visible only when no edge crosses the segment between them. |
| E-MP-04 | the clockwise angle used by the sweep is forced to 0 whenever the two directions agree in one coordinate (for example a vertex at exactly the height of the sweep point). | the angle is 0 only for equal directions. Visibility lines can change where a vertex and the start, goal or another vertex share an <i>x</i> or a <i>y</i> coordinate exactly. |
| E-MP-06 | a line that passes exactly through corners of a grown obstacle, or along contacts, is never counted as blocked: when start and goal line up with two corners of an obstacle the path goes straight through it (scene B1: length 4.00). | the straight start–goal line and every line of the graph are also tested against the interiors of all grown obstacles and dropped when they pass through one; touching a corner or running along an edge stays allowed. The path goes around the obstacle (scene B1: 4.36), or "No path exists." is shown. |

## Probabilistic Roadmap Method (`demos/prm/`)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| E-PR-01 | the search named A* adds the distance of a node to itself (always 0) as its estimate, so it is Dijkstra's algorithm. | the estimate is the distance from the node to the goal (A*). The path found has the same length; between equally short paths another one may be drawn. |
| E-PR-04 | the start and the goal are each tried against their single nearest sample only: when that one connection is blocked, "no path possible" is shown although other nearby samples connect to the roadmap. | up to ten nearest samples within the connection radius are tried, nearest first, as when the roadmap itself is built. |
| E-PR-05 | a start or goal that is in collision still gets a direct "path" to a configuration closer than the connection radius (the direct test comes before the collision tests and never tests its end points). | a direct path needs a start and a goal that are not in collision; otherwise "no path possible" is shown. |

## Robot Singularities in Three-Link Manipulators (`demos/robot-singularities/`)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| E-RS-01 | the angular Jacobian of the spherical wrist has −cos <i>q</i><sub>2</sub> in its last entry; the third joint axis of this robot points along +cos <i>q</i><sub>2</sub>, so the angular manipulability ellipsoid of the wrist is drawn with a wrong orientation. | the entry is +cos <i>q</i><sub>2</sub>: the ellipsoid is oriented along the true joint axes. The singular values and the singular sets do not change. |
| E-RS-02 | for the spherical wrist with "Linear" the singular set in the workspace is drawn as a sphere of radius 0.2 around (0, 0, 1). | the sphere has radius 1: the end point of this robot moves on the unit sphere around (0, 0, 1), and every configuration is singular. |
| E-RS-03 | a joint slider pushed past ±π jumps by 6.28 instead of 2π: the robot turns by 0.0032 rad at the jump and the value leaves the slider grid (1.01π becomes −3.10699). | the jump is 2π (1.01π becomes −0.99π = −3.11018): the robot does not move at the jump. |

## Breadth-First Search Robot Motion Planning (`demos/bfs-motion-planning/`)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| E-BF-02 | a diagonal step of the grid costs 1.41, so every diagonal is counted 0.3 % too short and the "path length" label with it. | a diagonal step costs √2 = 1.41421…; the cost map, the label and, where two routes are almost equally long, the chosen route follow. |
| E-BF-03 | an unreachable goal gives a one-cell "path": the arm jumps to the goal and the label reads "path length = ∞ rads"; a start inside an obstacle region is searched from as if it were free. | the label reads "no path exists" and the arm stays at the start; nothing is searched from a start inside an obstacle region. |
| E-BF-04 | a diagonal step is taken even between two blocked cells, so a path can pass through the corner where two obstacle cells meet. | such a diagonal step is not taken; the path goes around the corner. |
| E-BF-05 | the start and goal glyphs are both red or both green, according to whether the arm at its current position on the path collides. | each glyph is red when its own configuration collides and green otherwise. |
| E-BF-07 | a start or goal exactly on the edge of the phase space can be given a cell outside the grid (row 0 or row L + 1 for a typed non-integer Q with an odd grid size), which breaks the search. | the cell index is kept inside the grid (1 … L). |

## First-Order Transfer Functions in Process Control (`demos/first-order-process-control/`, since v0.1.37)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |

| E-FO-01 | sinusoidal input: the table gives the phase shift −ϕ = ArcTan[ω τ] with the unit "min", but it is an angle in radians (the time lag is ϕ/ω, equal to it only at ω = 1: at ω = 3.5 the table says 1.5 min, the lag is 0.43 min). | the phase shift is shown in rad, and a row "time lag ϕ/ω" gives the lag in minutes. |
| E-FO-02 | ramp input: the table's "time constant τ" is the vertical gap between input and response at <i>t</i> = 10/<i>a</i> (7.3 at τ = 5, <i>a</i> = 3), which is neither τ nor constant, and the τ marker is drawn there. | the table shows τ (the time by which the response lags the ramp once the transient has died away), and the τ marker is the horizontal lag at the response's value at <i>t</i> = 10. |
| E-FO-03 | sinusoidal input: "amplitude output <i>B</i>" is the first maximum of the response, which still contains the decaying transient (0.91 at the opening settings), so the amplitude ratio (0.3) is not that of the sinusoid the output settles to. | <i>B</i> = <i>K a</i>/√(ω²τ² + 1), the amplitude of the steady sinusoid (0.59), and the ratio <i>B</i>/<i>A</i> = 1/√(ω²τ² + 1) (0.2). The markers in the plot stay at the first maximum. |

## Determine If a Truss Can Be Solved (`demos/truss-solvability/`, since v0.1.40)

| Finding | The original (kept) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| E-TD-01 | the verdict is "solvable" whenever variables − equations ≤ 0. Without the support at joint B and with rollers at A and E there are 14 equations but only 13 unknowns (difference −1): the truss is a mechanism (it rolls sideways) and cannot be solved, yet it is called "solvable". Counting alone also cannot tell a well-placed set of supports from a badly placed one. | the verdict comes from the rank of the joint-balance equations (shared/truss.js): "solvable" when the equations determine every member force and reaction, "statically indeterminate" when there are more unknowns than independent equations, and "unstable (a mechanism)" when the supports or members cannot hold the truss still. The counts above stay as in the original. |
